name: Sanskrit
blurb: The language of the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa and Kālidāsa, and a distant cousin of Latin and Greek.
facts: saṃskṛta means 'put together' or 'refined', as opposed to the everyday Prākrits people actually spoke.
Pāṇini described the whole language in under 4,000 terse rules around the 4th century BC. Grammarians still use them.
Sanskrit has no script of its own. It was written in Brāhmī, Grantha, Śāradā and dozens more before printing made Devanagari the norm.
pitā, mātā and devaḥ are cousins of Latin pater, māter and deus, all inherited from Proto-Indo-European.
India's national motto, Satyameva Jayate, is a line from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad. You will learn it in unit 6.
English borrowed avatar, karma, mantra and yoga from Sanskrit.

guide.p: Devanagari writes syllables. A consonant letter on its own already carries a short a: क is ka, not k.
After a consonant a vowel becomes a small sign instead of a full letter. The i sign is written before the consonant but said after it. Not shown in the list: ऊ ū, ऐ ai and औ au.
The small stroke ् (virāma) removes the built-in a. Consonants with no vowel between them usually fuse into one cluster.
ं (anusvāra) nasalises the vowel before it, written ṃ. ः (visarga) is a soft breath after the vowel, written ḥ. Both sit at the end of countless words.

A line over a vowel makes it long: ā is held twice as long as a. c is always as in 'church'. A dot under t, d or n means the tongue curls back; ś is English sh and ṣ a curled-back sh. An h after a consonant is a puff of breath: ph is p plus breath, never f.

items.note: A vowel r. Most people today say it ri, as in Kṛṣṇa.
The two dots ः are a breath echoing the vowel: aḥ sounds like a-ha.

units.title: Namaste
units.about: Greet people and say who they are

guide.p: Sanskrit has no articles, and 'is' is usually left out. Two words side by side already make a sentence.
Masculine nouns in -a end in -aḥ when they are the subject. Feminine nouns end in -ā or -ī.
ca 'and' follows the word it adds, or each word in turn.

Sanskrit words change their last sound to suit the next word. This is called sandhi. For now every word appears as if said on its own (in pausa), the way dictionaries and many textbooks start. Sandhi begins in unit 4.

items.note: namaḥ 'a bow' + te 'to you'. Said with palms together.
Still a title of respect for great scholars.

units.title: Gṛham
units.about: Family, animals and the object ending

guide.p: The object of a verb changes its ending: -aḥ becomes -am, -ā becomes -ām, -ī becomes -īm.
paśyati is 'he sees', 'she sees' or 'it sees'. The verb usually comes last, but the endings, not the order, show who does what.
Some nouns, like gṛham, are neuter. They end in -am whether they are subject or object.
An adjective takes its noun's ending: śvetaḥ with masculine nouns, śvetā with feminine, śvetam with neuter. After the noun, with no verb, it says what the noun is like.
pitā and mātā follow an older pattern: as objects they become pitaram and mātaram. They are cousins of Latin pater and māter.

items.note: Feminine kṛṣṇā, neuter kṛṣṇam. Also the name Kṛṣṇa, 'the dark one'.

alt: the daughter sees a dark cat

units.title: Dinacaryā
units.about: Everyday verbs, I and you, and sandhi

guide.p: The ending shows the person: -āmi 'I', -asi 'you', -ati 'he, she, it'. aham and tvam are added only for emphasis.
The place you go to takes the object ending. No word for 'to' is needed. na 'not' usually stands right before the verb.
From this unit on, words join up as in real Sanskrit. A final -m before a consonant becomes ṃ (ं). Before a vowel or at the end of a sentence it stays m.
-aḥ turns into -o before a voiced sound: g j d b n m y r l v h. Before k or p, and at the end, it stays aḥ. saḥ simply drops its ḥ before any consonant.

items.note: I go: gacchāmi. You go: gacchasi.
Also 'result': the fruit of an action.

guide.p: Masculine and neuter nouns in -a take -asya for 'of'. The owner usually comes first.
mama 'my' and tava 'your' are the 'of' forms of aham and tvam. Feminine nouns take -āyāḥ or -yāḥ: bālāyāḥ 'of the girl', nadyāḥ 'of the river'.
Nouns like agniḥ and vāyuḥ turn ḥ into r before a voiced sound.
Before c, ḥ becomes ś. Before t it becomes s, which is how namaḥ te 'a bow to you' became namaste.
In Devanagari a word ending in a consonant normally runs into the next one: अग्निर्ज्वलति. Here words stay apart, with ् on the bare consonant, so each tile is one word.

items.note: From div 'to shine'. A cousin of Latin deus.
Also Agni, the fire god. A cousin of Latin ignis.
Also Vāyu, god of the wind.
Literally 'carries'. Said of the wind, it means 'blows'.

units.title: Subhāṣitāni
units.about: Famous lines from the Upaniṣads and beyond

guide.p: satyam eva jayate is from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (3.1.6) and is India's national motto. jayate is a middle-voice form of jayati 'conquers'. Devanagari usually runs it together as सत्यमेव जयते.

Two vowels across a word boundary melt into one, and the words are written as one: vasudhā + eva becomes vasudhaiva. Such a fused pair stays one tile. vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam ends a verse of the Mahā Upaniṣad (6.71–73), also found in the Hitopadeśa: only the small-minded ask who is kin, for the generous the whole earth is family.

dharma is duty, law, right conduct and the order of things all at once. ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ occurs several times in the Mahābhārata. dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ, 'dharma, protected, protects', is Manusmṛti 8.15.
The bare verb stem gives an order: vada 'speak!', cara 'walk, practise!'. satyaṃ vada dharmaṃ cara is a teacher's charge to departing students in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11.1).

tat tvam asi is the refrain of a father teaching his son in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.8.7). tat is the neuter of saḥ, and asi is 'you are'. vidyā dadāti vinayam comes from the preface of the Hitopadeśa, a book of animal fables.

items.note: From vasu 'wealth': the giver of riches.
asmi 'I am', asi 'you are', asti 'he is'.

units.title: Yātrā
units.about: Travel by chariot: with, to and from

guide.p: Sanskrit has eight cases. You already know the subject, the object and 'of'. This unit adds three more, each a single ending where English needs a preposition.
The instrumental says what something is done with or by. Masculine and neuter nouns in -a take -ena. Feminines in -ā take -ayā, and those in -ī take -yā. saha 'with' follows it.
An r, ṛ or ṣ earlier in the same word turns a later n into ṇ, unless a consonant such as t, d, c, ś or s comes between. So putra gives putreṇa, but ratha gives rathena.

The dative marks who something is given to or done for. Masculine and neuter nouns in -a take -āya; feminines take -āyai or -yai. namaḥ 'homage' takes it too. namaḥ śivāya, 'homage to Śiva', is the five-syllable prayer of Śiva's devotees.
The ablative says where something comes from. Masculine and neuter nouns in -a take -āt. Feminines use the same form as 'of': bālāyāḥ 'from the girl', nadyāḥ 'from the river'.

A final t becomes d before a vowel or before g, d, b, y, r or v. Before k, p, t or s, and at the end of a sentence, it stays t. Before other sounds it changes in other ways, which you will meet later.

items.note: Follows a noun in the instrumental.
The same word as in namaste.

units.title: Āśramaḥ
units.about: Life in the hermitage: 'in', plurals and full tables

guide.p: The locative says where. Masculine and neuter nouns in -a take -e; feminines take -āyām or -yām.
In the plural, subjects in -aḥ and -ā both end in -āḥ, neuters in -am end in -āni, and -ī becomes -yaḥ. The verb ending for 'they' is -anti, and santi means 'they are' or 'there are'.
vayam 'we' takes -āmaḥ and yūyam 'you all' takes -atha. With -āmi, -asi, -ati and -anti, that completes the present tense.

-āḥ simply drops its ḥ before a vowel or a voiced consonant, and the words stay apart. Before k or p it stays, and before t it becomes s, just like -aḥ. Vowels count as voiced, so ṛṣiḥ becomes ṛṣir before a vowel too.
ex: the sons live in the city
the sage lives in the hermitage

guide.p: Sanskrit also has a dual for exactly two: devau 'two gods', bāle 'two girls'. It fills a column in the tables below and returns with compounds in unit 11.

With the locative you have met seven cases. The eighth, the vocative, is for calling someone: deva 'O god!'. The full tables for -a and -ā nouns are at the end of this guidebook and on the Reference page.

units.title: Itihāsaḥ
units.about: Tell the past with -ta and the imperfect

guide.p: Adding -ta, sometimes -ita, to a verb root makes a word meaning 'gone', 'done', 'seen'. It takes adjective endings (-aḥ, -ā, -am) and is the everyday way to tell the past. You met one in unit 6: rakṣitaḥ 'protected'.
With verbs of going, the -ta form simply agrees with whoever went.

With other verbs the -ta form is passive. The thing done is the subject and the -ta form agrees with it, while the doer goes in the instrumental. Where English says 'the king killed the tiger', Sanskrit says 'the tiger was killed by the king'.
The pronouns have instrumentals too: mayā 'by me', tvayā 'by you', tena 'by him', tayā 'by her'.
Stories also use the imperfect. Put a- in front of the verb and shorten the endings: -am 'I', -aḥ 'you', -at 'he, she', -an 'they'. āsīt 'there was' is the imperfect of asti.
Before a, the ending -aḥ becomes -o and swallows the a. The lost a is marked ' (ऽ, avagraha), as in 'gne in the Ṛgveda story. Before any other vowel, -aḥ just loses its ḥ and the words stay apart.

units.title: Prabhātam
units.about: Chain actions with -tvā and say 'to do' with -tum

guide.p: The gerund ends in -tvā and never changes. It is an action the subject finishes before the main verb, where English says 'and', 'after' or 'having'.
ex: he sees the tiger and runs

guide.p: When the verb has a prefix such as ā- 'towards' or upa- 'near', the gerund ends in -ya instead.

The infinitive ends in -tum and never changes. It says what someone wants or is able to do, or why they do something. Like the Latin supine in -tum, it was once the object form of a verbal noun in -tu.
-ta, -tvā and -tum attach to the same root, so learn them as a set. Some roots change shape along the way: dṛś 'see' gives dṛṣṭa, dṛṣṭvā, draṣṭum, and pā 'drink' gives pīta, pītvā, pātum.
icchati 'wants' and śaknoti 'can' take an infinitive. śaknoti belongs to a group of verbs with the endings -nomi, -noṣi, -noti.

items.note: I can: śaknomi. You can: śaknoṣi.

units.title: Samāsaḥ
units.about: Build long words: tatpuruṣa, dvandva, bahuvrīhi

guide.p: A compound strings words together, and only the last one takes an ending. The others appear as bare stems: rāja- is the stem of the word for 'king', and pitā and mātā become pitṛ- and mātṛ-. Devanagari writes a compound as one word, and so does this course.

The first part relates to the second as if it had a case ending, most often 'of': a rājaputraḥ is a king's son, a devālayaḥ a god's dwelling. When the first part simply describes the second, as in mahārājaḥ 'great king', the compound is called a karmadhāraya. Vowels meeting inside a compound melt as in unit 6.
A dvandva joins its parts with 'and'. Two people make a dual ending in -au, and the verb takes the dual ending -taḥ. Two things make a neuter dual in -e.

A bahuvrīhi describes someone by what they have. The word itself means 'having much rice', that is, rich. nīlakaṇṭhaḥ 'whose throat is blue' is Śiva, who drank the poison churned up from the ocean. daśarathaḥ 'having ten chariots' is the name of Rāma's father.

Sending his students home, the teacher in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11.2) tells each one mātṛdevo bhava, 'be one whose god is your mother'. bhava is the command form of bhavati. atithidevo bhava from the same passage became the slogan of an Indian tourism campaign.
sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā opens Bhagavad Gītā 2.38, where Kṛṣṇa urges Arjuna to fight with an even mind. same is the dual of samaḥ 'equal', agreeing with sukhaduḥkhe, and kṛtvā is the -tvā form of kṛ.

items.note: nīla 'blue' + kaṇṭha 'throat'. A name of Śiva, and a word for the peacock.

units.title: Ślokāḥ
units.about: The epic verse and lines everyone quotes

guide.p: Most of the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa and the Gītā is in one metre, the śloka: four quarters (pāda) of eight syllables, printed as two lines of sixteen. A quarter is usually a phrase on its own, so the lines in this unit are single quarters or half-verses.

A syllable is heavy if its vowel is long (ā ī ū ṝ e ai o au) or is followed by ṃ, ḥ or two consonants; otherwise it is light. In the second and fourth quarters, syllables five to seven run light, heavy, light, so every couplet ends with the same lilt. The last syllable of a quarter can be either.
ex: saṃ bha vā mi | yu ge yu ge

guide.p: The Rāmāyaṇa tells how the first śloka was made. The sage Vālmīki saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of krauñca birds, and his grief burst out as a curse in verse: mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṃ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ, 'hunter, may you find no rest for endless years'. Repeating it, his students marvelled that grief (śoka) had become verse: śokaḥ ślokatvam āgataḥ (1.2.39). -tva makes abstract nouns, like English -ness.

yataḥ 'from where' is answered by tataḥ 'from there'. yato dharmas tato jayaḥ, 'where dharma is, there is victory', recurs more than a dozen times in the Mahābhārata (for example 6.21.11) and is the motto of India's Supreme Court.

Poets arrange words to fit the metre and fill quarters with small words like hi 'for, indeed' and khalu 'indeed'. Trust the endings, not the order. You will also meet plural endings of other noun types: sādhūnām 'of the good', duṣkṛtām 'of evildoers', karmasu 'in actions'. A repeated locative means 'in every': yuge yuge 'age after age'.

udyamena hi sidhyanti and na hi suptasya siṃhasya make one couplet in the preface of the Hitopadeśa. paritrāṇāya sādhūnām is Kṛṣṇa explaining why he takes birth again and again, Bhagavad Gītā 4.8, and yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam is Gītā 2.50. śarīram ādyaṃ khalu dharmasādhanam comes from Kālidāsa's Kumārasambhava (5.33), in a longer metre of twelve syllables.

items.note: Ends in -uḥ like vāyuḥ. 'Of the good': sādhūnām.
Also 'yoke', a cousin of English yoke.
